title: ijCSCL—a journal for research in CSCL
summary_haiku: The International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (ijCSCL) was established to advance the maturing CSCL field by providing a peer-reviewed publication venue for an increasingly global research community. The journal aims to foster interdisciplinary collaboration, develop CSCL-specific theories and methodologies, and disseminate high-quality research through open-access online platforms alongside traditional publication formats.

title: The CSCL community in its ﬁrst decade: development, continuity, connectivity
summary_haiku: The CSCL community's first decade (1995–2005) demonstrates growth and increasing internationalization despite low individual continuity. Using quantitative analysis of conference proceedings, participant lists, and program committees combined with qualitative surveys, researchers found that while 79% of authors contributed to only one conference, international connectivity grew substantially through citations and co-authorships across countries, with conference location rotation and diverse program committee composition supporting this development.

title: A relational, indirect, meso-level approach to CSCL design in the next decade
authors: Chris Jones & Lone Dirckinck<Holmfeld & Berner Lindstro¨m
summary_haiku: This theoretical paper proposes a relational approach to CSCL design, arguing that technology, affordances, and infrastructure should be understood as emerging through relationships rather than as fixed properties. Drawing on two European research networks, the authors advocate for meso-level analysis bridging micro-group and macro-institutional processes, and recommend indirect design strategies that acknowledge contingency in how learners enact technological affordances within networked learning environments.

title: Students assessing their own collaborative knowledge building
authors: Eddy Y.C. Lee & Carol K.K. Chan & Jan van Aalst
summary_haiku: This study examined how electronic portfolio assessments guided by knowledge-building principles support collaborative inquiry in computer forums. Using a quasi-experimental design with 119 ninth-grade students across three Knowledge Forum conditions, researchers found that students receiving portfolios with knowledge-building principles demonstrated deeper inquiry, more high-level questions, and superior conceptual understanding compared to peers using forums alone or portfolios without principles. Portfolio scores predicted essay performance beyond individual participation metrics, suggesting portfolios effectively capture distributed, progressive knowledge advancement.

title: Situating CoWeb: a scholarship of application
summary_haiku: Researchers developed CoWeb, a wiki-based platform for collaborative learning, and deployed it across diverse academic contexts at Georgia Tech. Through design-based research, they found that collaborative learning success depends critically on cultural compatibility: CoWeb succeeded in architecture and composition where collaboration aligned with disciplinary values, but failed in STEM courses due to competitive cultures. By redesigning an introductory computing course around collaborative principles, they overcame these barriers, demonstrating that culture can be intentionally shaped to support technology adoption.

title: R-U-Typing-2-Me? Evolving a chat tool to increase understanding in learning activities
authors: Hugo Fuks & Mariano Pimentel & Carlos Jose´ Pereira de Lucena
summary_haiku: This research investigates "Chat Confusion"—difficulties following conversations when multiple participants communicate simultaneously in chat tools used for educational debates. Through iterative design-based development, researchers identified six key problems: co-text loss, dynamics interruption, message overload, lack-of-visibility-of-turn-in-progress, reading difficulties, and decontextualization. Successive Mediated Chat versions implemented targeted solutions including message threading, structured conversation techniques, publication queues, interface improvements, and session history. Case studies demonstrated that combining structured dynamics with interface enhancements effectively reduced confusion and improved understanding in online learning activities.

title: A dialogic understanding of the relationship between CSCL and teaching thinking skills
summary_haiku: # Summary Wegerif argues that dialogue itself constitutes the primary thinking skill underlying creativity and learning-to-learn. Through literature review and case studies using Raven's reasoning tests, he demonstrates that teaching dialogue as an end in itself—rather than as a tool for knowledge construction—promotes general thinking skills. He proposes a dialogic interpretative framework for CSCL that emphasizes opening, deepening, and broadening reflective spaces through technology-supported dialogue.

title: Building knowledge in the classroom, building knowledge in the CSCL community
summary_haiku: This editorial introduces the International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning's second issue, presenting six articles addressing knowledge building in classrooms through collaborative learning with digital tools. The collection spans international research examining institutional context, design principles, narrative analysis, activity structures, and synchronous communication frameworks, demonstrating how pedagogy, technology, content, and theory must develop together in CSCL research.

title: Approaching institutional contexts: Systemic versus dialogic research in CSCL
summary_haiku: # Summary This article distinguishes between systemic and dialogic research approaches in CSCL to address how institutional contexts shape tool meanings and functions. Systemic approaches identify variable correlations affecting collaboration and outcomes, while dialogic approaches examine how meanings emerge through social interaction. The authors argue that dialogic analysis of sequential activities reveals why CSCL applications often fail in ordinary classrooms, demonstrating that understanding institutional practice transformation requires attention to how participants actively constitute contexts through their actions.

title: Collaborative knowledge building using the Design Principles Database
summary_haiku: The Design Principles Database (DPD) supports collaborative knowledge building among educational technology researchers through a structured system of interconnected design features and principles at multiple abstraction levels. Using design-based research methodology across three iterations of a peer-evaluation activity, the study demonstrates how researchers extract principles from literature, test them in practice, and contribute refined knowledge back to the community database, exemplifying second-order collaborative learning environments.

title: Co-reﬂection in online learning: Collaborative critical thinking as narrative
summary_haiku: This study examined two graduate students' learning in an online action research course using narrative analysis. The research identifies co-reflection—a collaborative critical thinking process combining cognitive and affective interactions with relationship building—as central to knowledge co-construction. Two co-reflection types emerged: tacit (indirect, subtle) and active (explicit, discursive). Simple, flexible software tools effectively supported inquiry learning by accommodating diverse communication and learning styles.

title: Knowledge-building activity structures in Japanese elementary science pedagogy
authors: Jun Oshima & Ritsuko Oshima & Isao Murayama & Shigenori Inagaki & Makiko Takenaka & Tomokazu Yamamoto & Etsuji Yamaguchi & Hayashi Nakayama
summary_haiku: # Summary This design study examined how to transform Japanese elementary science classrooms into knowledge-building communities by integrating traditional activity structures with CSCL technology. Across two consecutive years, researchers refined lesson designs using Knowledge Forum to support idea-centered, collaborative inquiry. Results showed that improving task authenticity and participatory structures—particularly blending online and offline communication—significantly enhanced students' collective knowledge advancement and engagement with conceptual artifacts compared to initial implementations.

title: Supporting synchronous collaborative learning: A generic, multi-dimensional model
summary_haiku: Lonchamp proposes Omega+, a multi-dimensional model-based generic synchronous collaborative learning environment addressing limited applicability of existing CSCL systems. The system uses separate explicit models for collaborative situations, interactions, processes, and performance monitoring, enabling flexible combinations of scaffolding techniques. Evaluation occurs through functional equivalence demonstrations and a dedicated web platform supporting real-world usage analysis and teacher customization.

title: ERRATUM Students assessing their own collaborative knowledge building
authors: Eddy Y.C. Lee & Carol K.K. Chan & Jan van Aalst
summary_haiku: This study examined how knowledge-building portfolios and principles scaffold collaborative inquiry in computer forums. Using a quasi-experimental design with 119 ninth-grade students across three Knowledge Forum conditions, researchers found that students guided by knowledge-building principles demonstrated deeper inquiry, more high-level questions, and superior conceptual understanding compared to peers using forums alone or with portfolios only. Portfolio scores predicted domain understanding beyond individual participation measures, suggesting portfolios effectively characterize and foster collective knowledge advances.

title: EDITORIAL Focusing on participation in group meaning making
summary_haiku: This editorial proposes intersubjective meaning making as a unifying theoretical focus for CSCL research, arguing it better captures collaborative learning phenomena than traditional frameworks. The issue presents four articles exemplifying this approach: anchored discussion using quantitative analysis, networked handhelds supporting group interaction, and social network analysis combined with qualitative methods to examine student participation processes.

title: Technology affordances for intersubjective meaning making: A research agenda for CSCL Daniel D. Suthers
authors: making: A research agenda for CSCL Daniel D. Suthers
summary_haiku: Suthers proposes intersubjective meaning making—how groups jointly compose interpretations of dynamically evolving contexts—as CSCL's integrating research agenda. Through conceptual analysis, he argues that technology should be designed as fundamentally social to afford such meaning-making processes. He advocates hybrid methodologies combining experimental, descriptive, and design approaches, with "uptake" relations serving as a boundary object enabling dialogue across theoretical traditions.

title: The affordance of anchored discussion for the collaborative processing of academic texts
authors: J. van der Pol & W. Admiraal & P.R.J. Simons
summary_haiku: Anchored discussion systems, which integrate texts directly into online forums with message anchoring capabilities, promote more text-focused and constructive collaboration than traditional forum discussion. Comparing these systems with standard discussion boards in a pedagogy course, the study found anchored discussion produced more meaning-oriented discourse, more efficient communication, and fewer social digressions, making it more suitable for collaborative academic text comprehension among undergraduate students.

title: Code talk: Student discourse and participation with networked handhelds
summary_haiku: Networked handheld computers in a middle school mathematics classroom expanded collaborative problem-solving participation beyond traditional discourse. Through interactional analysis of two student groups using the Code Breaker cryptography software, the study found that students demonstrating largest achievement gains gave more instructions and responded less frequently. Importantly, shared mathematical objects across devices enabled non-discursive participation forms, allowing lower-status students to contribute meaningfully despite limited verbal participation.

title: Studying participation networks in collaboration using mixed methods
authors: AlejandraMartínez & Yannis Dimitriadis & Eduardo Gómez-Sánchez & Bartolomé Rubia-Avi & Iván Jorrín-Abellán & Jose A. Marcos
summary_haiku: This study validates a mixed-evaluation method combining social network analysis with qualitative and quantitative approaches to assess participatory learning in CSCL contexts. Applied across three diverse scenarios—blended learning, distance learning, and synchronous collaboration—the method demonstrates flexibility and appropriateness for measuring interaction structures. Results confirm that integrating multiple data sources and analysis techniques provides efficient, reliable evaluation while remaining accessible to practitioners, though resource demands remain substantial.

title: Social practices of
summary_haiku: Computer-supported collaborative learning requires students to develop effective social practices to compensate for missing nonverbal cues in virtual environments. This editorial examines four empirical studies investigating how groups establish interaction patterns for dialogue, mathematical inquiry, blended learning dynamics, and consistent communication practices, demonstrating that social practices are central to both individual and collaborative cognition.

title: From dialogue to monologue and back: Middle spaces in computer-mediated learning
summary_haiku: This study develops a framework distinguishing communication interfaces supporting dialogue from information interfaces supporting monologue in computer-mediated learning. Through design-based research with the Knowledge Integration Environment, the authors examine how students transition between these modes using SpeakEasy and SenseMaker tools. Case analyses reveal that successful learners strategically moved between dialogue and monologue, reflecting on ideas and identifying knowledge gaps, while less successful learners failed to leverage these transitions, suggesting that "middle spaces" bridging both modes enhance learning trajectories.

title: Knowledge building in mathematics: Supporting collaborative learning in pattern problems
summary_haiku: Grade 4 students using Knowledge Forum, a collaborative online platform, demonstrated sophisticated mathematical reasoning when solving pattern generalization problems. Students found multiple algebraic rules per problem, revised their conjectures over weeks, and increasingly provided detailed justifications—behaviors rarely observed in traditional instruction. Knowledge-building principles of epistemic agency and idea improvement fostered this inquiry orientation, with students spontaneously recognizing structural similarities across problems.

title: Electronic [re]constitution of groups: Group dynamics from face-to-face to an online setting
authors: Lynn Clouder & Jayne Dalley & Julian Hargreaves & Sally Parkes & Julie Sellars & Jane Toms
summary_haiku: This three-year case study examined how group dynamics change when physiotherapy students transition from face-to-face to online collaboration during clinical placements. Using action research with six seminar groups, researchers analyzed discussion forums, focus groups, and evaluations. Findings reveal that group dynamics remain relatively stable across contexts once established face-to-face, though individual participation may shift online. Social presence proves essential for positive dynamics, yet groups must transcend sociability to develop cognitive presence and deeper learning. Effective facilitation significantly influences outcomes, particularly when managing emotionally charged discussions or low-engagement groups.

title: Consistent practices in artifact-mediated collaboration
summary_haiku: This study examined how dyads collaboratively solve problems using flexible paper-based media while restricted to written communication. Through video analysis of six pairs discussing wicked problems, researchers identified invariant communicative practices across different materials and participants. Despite varied interaction styles and artifacts, consistent patterns emerged in managing attention, awareness, and ownership of contributions. Findings challenge conventional CSCL design assumptions and suggest that effective collaborative technologies should support flexible semiotic resources rather than rigid representational structures.

title: Welcome to the future: ijCSCL volume 2
summary_haiku: This editorial marks ijCSCL's second volume, celebrating the journal's establishment as a vital communication venue for the CSCL community. Nearly one hundred papers were submitted globally, reviewed by two hundred researchers, demonstrating the field's maturation. The journal serves dual purposes: formal publication and constructive peer feedback, advancing collaborative learning research through rigorous editorial processes and community engagement.

title: Community-based learning: The core competency of residential, research-based universities
authors: Gerhard Fischer & Markus Rohde & Volker Wulf
summary_haiku: Residential research universities can maintain competitive advantage against online education by adopting community-based learning grounded in socio-cultural theory. The authors present case studies from University of Colorado and University of Siegen demonstrating how integrating students into communities of practice through apprenticeships, peer collaboration, and regional industry partnerships creates meaningful learning experiences that transcend traditional instructionist models, requiring significant cultural change and faculty risk-taking.

title: Patterns as a paradigm for theory in community-based learning
summary_haiku: Carroll and Farooq propose design patterns as a theoretical framework for understanding community-based IT learning. Through 12 years of participatory action research with volunteer organizations, they present two patterns: "Informal Developmental Learning" addresses lack of IT control through reflection, analysis, and enactment; "Scaffolded Documentation" manages knowledge loss from volunteer turnover via technology assessment, contingency planning, and lightweight documentation. Patterns serve as middle-level abstractions capturing recurring problems and solutions intelligible to practitioners themselves.

title: A rating scheme for assessing the quality of computer-supported collaboration processes
authors: Anne Meier & Hans Spada & Nikol Rummel
summary_haiku: Researchers developed a nine-dimension rating scheme for assessing computer-supported collaboration quality by combining qualitative analysis of student dialogue with theoretical frameworks. Applied to 40 dyads solving interdisciplinary patient cases via videoconferencing, the scheme demonstrated satisfactory inter-rater reliability and successfully detected instructional effects on collaboration processes, offering an efficient alternative to time-consuming transcription-based coding methods.

title: Investigating patterns of interaction in networked learning and
authors: Maarten de Laat & Vic Lally & Lasse Lipponen & Robert-Jan Simons
summary_haiku: Social Network Analysis (SNA) combined with content analysis and critical event recall provides valuable insights into networked learning communities. This multi-method study examined interaction patterns in an online master's program, revealing how participant roles and network density evolve over time. SNA effectively visualizes collaboration structures and identifies central versus peripheral members, complementing traditional qualitative methods to deepen understanding of computer-supported collaborative learning dynamics.

title: Barriers to online critical discourse
summary_haiku: This qualitative case study examined barriers to critical discourse in online forums within a 15-week graduate humanities course. Through observation and interviews with five distance students, researchers identified three key obstacles: students held competing orientations toward the conference (some seeking critique, others socioemotional support), perceived critiques as personal attacks, and viewed critical discourse as burdensome for participation marks. Structured learning activities with defined roles and assessment methods reflecting engagement effort could mitigate these barriers.

title: A double issue for CSCL 2007
authors: Gerry Stahl & Daniel D. Suthers & Friedrich Hesse
summary_haiku: This editorial introduces a double issue of the International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning coinciding with CSCL 2007. It presents papers organized around two "flash themes": scripting in collaborative learning environments and argumentation in CSCL. The collection features empirical studies employing mixed methods—quantitative coding, controlled experiments, and qualitative analysis—demonstrating how structured scripts and argumentative dialogue support knowledge construction in computer-mediated collaborative learning contexts.

title: Contextual perspective in analysing collaborative knowledge construction of two small groups in web-based discussion
summary_haiku: This study presents a methodology for analyzing collaborative knowledge construction in asynchronous web-based discussions by examining two student groups' thematic structure, communicative functions, and contextual resources. Comparing novice and experienced teacher-education students, findings reveal that different backgrounds influenced how groups created and interpreted context, negotiated meanings, and selected resources—novices relied on course material and peer discussion, while experienced students drew primarily on personal teaching experience.

title: Supporting collaborative learning and problem-solving in a constraint-based CSCL environment for UML class diagrams
authors: Nilufar Baghaei & Antonija Mitrovic & Warwick Irwin
summary_haiku: COLLECT-UML is a constraint-based intelligent tutoring system that teaches UML class diagram design while supporting collaborative learning. Using meta-constraints to model collaboration alongside domain constraints, the system provides feedback on both problem-solving and teamwork. Evaluation studies with 48 students showed significant improvements in UML knowledge and collaboration skills, with experimental group participants acquiring greater declarative knowledge about effective collaboration and demonstrating more balanced, active participation.

title: Dealing with multiple documents on the WWW: The role of metacognition in the formation of documents models
summary_haiku: This study examined whether metacognitive prompting helps laypersons form documents models—integrated representations of content and sources—when researching medical information online. Using an experimental design with 79 participants assigned to groups receiving evaluation prompts, monitoring prompts, both, or neither, researchers found that monitoring prompts enhanced factual knowledge acquisition, while evaluation prompts improved source knowledge and source attribution in essays, supporting metacognition's importance in multiple-document comprehension.

title: Specifying computer-supported collaboration scripts
authors: Lars Kobbe & Armin Weinberger & Pierre Dillenbourg & Andreas Harrer & Raija Hämäläinen & Päivi Häkkinen & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: This paper proposes a comprehensive framework for specifying computer-supported collaboration scripts by consolidating prior approaches. Through conceptual analysis, the authors identify five core components (participants, activities, roles, resources, groups) and three mechanisms (task distribution, group formation, sequencing) that enable platform-independent script description. The framework facilitates systematic research, practical design, and computational formalization of collaborative learning scripts across diverse educational contexts.

title: Scripting by assigning roles: Does it improve knowledge construction in asynchronous discussion groups?
authors: Tammy Schellens & Hilde Van Keer & Bram De Wever & Martin Valcke
summary_haiku: This design-based research compared two cohorts of university students (N=223 and N=286) across consecutive academic years to examine whether assigning rotating roles in asynchronous discussion groups enhances knowledge construction. Using multilevel analysis of coded discussion transcripts and exam scores, results showed that role assignment significantly improved students' knowledge construction levels and final exam performance, with an effect size of 0.5 standard deviations. However, differential effects emerged by role type, with summarizers benefiting most.

title: Using graphical tools in a phased activity for enhancing dialogical skills: An example with Digalo
authors: Nathalie Muller Mirza & Valérie Tartas & Anne-Nelly Perret-Clermont & Jean-François de Pietro
summary_haiku: This study examined how university students developed argumentative and historical knowledge through a phased learning activity using Digalo, graphical argument-mapping software. Using descriptive analysis of two collective debates about the Valladolid Controversy, researchers found that students constructed complex understanding of the historical topic while developing sophisticated argument-counterargument-reply sequences. The software's visual representations and structured functionalities supported both topic meaning-making and argumentative processes, enabling students to elaborate justifications and integrate opposing perspectives into their reasoning.

title: How do argumentation diagrams compare when student pairs use them as a means for debate or as a tool for representing debate?
authors: Kristine Lund & Gaëlle Molinari & Arnauld Séjourné & Michael Baker
summary_haiku: This study compared two instructional approaches for using argumentation diagrams during online debates among 36 secondary students. Using the ADAM analysis method, researchers examined individual diagrams created before and after debate, plus collaborative diagrams produced during debate. Results revealed that students instructed to represent their chat debate in diagrams added more non-argumentative relations (examples, causes, consequences), while those using diagrams simultaneously during debate expressed more opinions about arguments. These findings suggest different cognitive mechanisms emerge depending on whether diagrams mediate debate or represent completed debate.

title: Argumentation in a changing world
authors: Baruch B. Schwarz & Reuma De Groot
summary_haiku: # Summary This design-based research study examined a seven-month history course using the Kishurim program, which promotes critical reasoning through dialogic argumentation supported by the Digalo graphic tool. While traditional measures of argumentative components showed no significant improvement, students demonstrated significant gains in openness, coherence, and decisiveness. Analysis of e-discussions revealed that these criteria better reflect the program's dialogic pedagogical principles than conventional skill-based metrics, suggesting new evaluation standards for collaborative learning environments.

title: Rainbow: A framework for analysing computer-mediated pedagogical debates
authors: Michael Baker & Jerry Andriessen & Kristine Lund & Marie van Amelsvoort & Matthieu Quignard
summary_haiku: Rainbow is a seven-category analytical framework for analyzing computer-mediated pedagogical debates in CSCL environments. Developed through pragma-dialectical theory and dialogue analysis, it identifies when students broaden and deepen understanding of debate spaces through argumentative interaction. The framework synthesizes existing approaches into coherent functional categories, validated across multiple collaborative learning tasks and communication media with strong inter-coder reliability.

title: CSCL and its flash themes
summary_haiku: Stahl examines how "flash themes"—coordinated collections of papers on emerging research topics—develop within the CSCL community through collaborative, iterative processes involving workshops, peer review, and journal publication. Using a dialectical metaphor of logs and fire, he argues that scientific ideas emerge not from individual minds but through situated, institutionally-mediated interactions among researchers, editors, and the broader academic community.

title: Using activity-oriented design methods to study collaborative knowledge-building in e-learning courses within higher education
summary_haiku: Activity-Oriented Design Methods (AODM) operationalize Activity Theory to analyze collaborative knowledge-building in e-learning courses. Using qualitative case study methodology, researchers applied AODM's six-stage framework to examine course design teams and students in online higher education. Findings revealed that peer collaboration, facilitated through small-group assignments and discussion guidelines, supported students' development of statistical knowledge through exploratory talk and iterative refinement of shared learning objects.

title: Future technology workshop: A collaborative method for the design of new learning technologies and activities
summary_haiku: The Future Technology Workshop (FTW) is a collaborative design method enabling participants with domain knowledge to envision and prototype interactions between current/future technologies and activities. Through seven structured sessions combining brainstorming, low-tech prototyping, role-play, and scenario analysis, participants progress from imagining far-future possibilities to grounding ideas in present constraints, ultimately generating implementable technology requirements. Successfully applied with children and adults across multiple projects, FTW provides cost-effective, pragmatic outcomes directly informing human-centered systems design.

title: Facilitating argumentative knowledge construction with computer-supported collaboration scripts
authors: Karsten Stegmann & Armin Weinberger & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: Computer-supported collaboration scripts significantly improve argumentative knowledge construction in online discussions. A 2×2 factorial study with 120 educational science students examined scripts supporting single argument construction and argumentation sequences. Results showed scripts substantially enhanced formal argument quality and argumentation sequence quality. Scripts also facilitated knowledge on argumentation but not domain-specific knowledge, suggesting learners focused effort on argumentation skills rather than content mastery.

title: The role of floor control and of ontology in argumentative activities with discussion-based tools
summary_haiku: This study examined how informal argumentative ontologies and floor control in synchronous e-discussions affect knowledge co-elaboration among 54 seventh-grade students using the Digalo tool. Using a 2×2 factorial design, researchers compared conditions with/without ontology and with/without floor control. Results showed that combining informal ontology with floor control produced significantly more relevant claims and arguments while reducing chat-style expressions and non-productive peer references, suggesting these design features facilitate collaborative knowledge construction.

title: Putting the pieces together: Online argumentation vee diagrams enhance thinking during discussions
authors: E. Michael Nussbaum & Denise L. Winsor & Yvette M. Aqui & Anne M. Poliquin
summary_haiku: Online argumentation vee diagrams (AVDs) significantly enhance students' ability to integrate opposing arguments in asynchronous discussions. Using a quasi-experimental design with 87 preservice teachers, students completing individual AVDs before discussions and collaborative group AVDs afterward demonstrated greater compromise-based reasoning and opinion change compared to controls. Scaffolding questions evaluating argument strength proved essential for effectiveness, suggesting structured support facilitates metacognitive reflection necessary for balanced argumentation.

title: The many levels of CSCL
summary_haiku: CSCL research operates across multiple interconnected social levels—individual, small group, and classroom—requiring integrated pedagogical designs that coordinate activities across these levels. Effective collaborative learning depends on understanding how constraints at institutional, domain, and technological levels intersect with group dynamics, necessitating both qualitative and quantitative multilevel analyses.

title: The mechanics of CSCL macro scripts
summary_haiku: Macro scripts structure collaborative learning by strategically distributing resources, roles, and knowledge among team members to increase interaction intensity. Using pedagogical design principles and computational data structure transformations, scripts trigger knowledge-productive interactions like argumentation and explanation. The SWISH model demonstrates how scripts engineer productive learning by creating controlled "splits" that require students to interact intensively to reach shared understanding.

title: What does it mean? Students’ procedural and conceptual problem solving in a CSCL environment designed within the field of science education
summary_haiku: This study examined procedural versus conceptual problem-solving in a CSCL environment where secondary students built a 3D insulin protein model using a codon table. Through interaction analysis of video-recorded collaborative sessions, researchers found that procedural problem-solving dominated student interactions, while conceptual knowledge construction occurred only when necessary for task completion. The authors conclude that institutional pressures to complete curriculum-based problems, combined with how the knowledge domain and tools were designed, prioritized procedural efficiency over deeper scientific understanding.

title: A Community of Practice among tutors enabling student participation in a seminar preparation
summary_haiku: A tutor community of practice overcame institutional barriers to implementing computer-supported collaborative learning in a Computer and Law seminar. Through informal collaboration and shared identity, tutors self-organized to design and conduct an educational experiment using JurMOO, a text-based virtual platform, for seminar preparation. This bottom-up approach enabled student participation and learning where top-down professor coordination had failed, demonstrating that tutor communities can effectively support educational innovation.

title: The need for considering multilevel analysis in CSCL research—An appeal for the use of more advanced statistical methods
summary_haiku: CSCL research involves hierarchically nested data—individuals within groups—yet standard statistical methods violate independence assumptions, causing alpha-error inflation. Multilevel modeling (MLM) addresses this by simultaneously analyzing individual and group levels, testing cross-level interactions between within-group predictors and between-group variables. However, MLM requires large sample sizes typically unavailable in CSCL studies, necessitating alternative approaches and careful reporting of intraclass correlations.

title: Group awareness and self-presentation in computer-supported information exchange
summary_haiku: This experimental study examined how group awareness tools and protective self-presentation (PSP) influence knowledge-sharing behavior in computer-supported information exchange. Using a laboratory task simulating a social dilemma, 119 participants worked in three conditions: control, group-feedback, and individual-feedback. Results showed that individual feedback identifying each participant's contributions significantly increased cooperation rates, particularly among high-PSP individuals. An interaction effect emerged: high protective self-presenters were most cooperative when identifiable but least cooperative anonymously, suggesting self-presentation concerns drive knowledge-sharing behavior in collaborative digital environments.

title: The strength of the lone wolf
summary_haiku: This editorial examines the dialectical relationship between individual and group in computer-supported collaborative learning. Through conceptual analysis of five research papers addressing wikis, group feedback, annotations, argumentation scripts, and macro-scripts, the author argues that CSCL technology must mediate the intersubjective-to-individual learning process. The papers demonstrate how specific tools shape both individual cognition and collaborative group practices.

title: A systemic and cognitive view on collaborative knowledge building with wikis
summary_haiku: This article presents a theoretical framework integrating Luhmann's systems theory with Piaget's equilibration theory to explain collaborative knowledge building in wikis. The model distinguishes between social and cognitive systems, analyzing how externalization and internalization processes enable learning through assimilation and accommodation. Empirical Wikipedia examples demonstrate that medium-level incongruities between individual knowledge and wiki content motivate equilibration activities, driving both individual learning and collaborative knowledge building through co-evolution of systems.

title: Supporting controversial CSCL discussions with augmented group awareness tools
summary_haiku: Augmented group awareness tools that aggregate and visualize learner ratings of discussion contributions can strengthen minority influence in collaborative learning. An experimental study with groups discussing controversial physics topics found that groups using rating-based awareness tools made significantly better decisions and showed higher individual learning than unsupported groups, particularly by shifting majority members toward scientifically correct minority viewpoints through enhanced informational influence.

title: Annotations and the collaborative digital library: Effects of an aligned annotation interface on student argumentation and reading strategies
summary_haiku: Aligned annotation interfaces—where reader comments appear in text margins—significantly enhance student critical thinking and argumentation. Two complementary studies found that annotations, particularly pairs presenting conflicting viewpoints, prompted students to move beyond passive comprehension toward active evaluation and perspective-taking. Students receiving annotated materials demonstrated reduced reliance on summary strategies and greater engagement with competing positions, suggesting annotations provide valuable scaffolding for developing critical reading and writing practices.

title: Appropriation of a shared workspace: Organizing principles and their application
summary_haiku: This case study examines how student groups appropriate a graphical shared workspace during computer-mediated argumentative discussion. Through micro-analysis of tool-mediated interactions, the researchers found that groups develop shared organizational principles through implicit negotiation of conventions. Four groups demonstrated distinct orientations—maintaining direct interaction, constructing personal reasoning, or submitting unrelated contributions—resulting in different principles for organizing contributions. The study reveals mutual shaping between students and tool, where early choices constrain later possibilities and strong graphical principles prove difficult to abandon.

title: Operationalizing macro-scripts in CSCL technological settings
summary_haiku: This article proposes SPAIRD, a conceptualization model for operationalizing CSCL macro-scripts—pedagogical activity structures that guide collaborative learning. The research identifies core design dimensions including script reification through technology, student presentation strategies, and uncertainties in script perception and enactment. SPAIRD disentangles structural models, implementation models, platform specifications, and student-oriented models while documenting design rationale. The analysis examines current technological approaches and advocates for flexible, model-based script engines supporting iterative design.

title: Explorations of participation in discourse
summary_haiku: This editorial examines how participation in discourse defines collaborative learning in CSCL research. It reviews studies analyzing student communication traces and discourse participation, highlighting challenges in automated analysis due to contextual dependencies. The articles featured demonstrate how technology design, scripting, and computational tools can support students' meaningful participation in disciplinary discourses across diverse learning contexts.

title: Analyzing collaborative learning processes automatically: Exploiting the advances of computational linguistics in
authors: Carolyn Rosé & Yi-Chia Wang & Yue Cui & Jaime Arguello & Karsten Stegmann & Armin Weinberger & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: Researchers applied computational linguistics text classification technology to automatically analyze collaborative learning discourse using a multi-dimensional coding scheme. Testing on 1,250 coded segments, they achieved acceptable reliability (Kappa ≥0.7) on several dimensions by designing linguistically-informed features reflecting thread structure and discourse context, demonstrating that feature engineering proved more effective than sophisticated algorithms for this task.

title: Context-oriented communication and the design of computer-supported discursive learning
summary_haiku: This theory-driven design experiment develops a context-oriented communication model to guide computer-supported discursive learning (CSDL) system design. Through iterative testing of the KOLUMBUS prototype across five classroom settings, researchers identified that integrating communicative annotations directly with segmented learning material as context significantly enhances mutual understanding in asynchronous discussions. The study extends traditional dyadic communication models by introducing the facilitator as a crucial third party, providing practical design guidelines emphasizing context integration, metadata support, and facilitation features.

title: Cultural practices in networked classroom learning environments
summary_haiku: Networked classroom simulations enable underserved secondary mathematics students to leverage cultural practices as learning resources. This case study examined the Gridlock Participatory Simulation, analyzing how coordination and co-construction activities—supported by multiple communication modes including informal language, gesture, and graphical representations—invited students to draw on community-based interaction patterns while engaging in rigorous mathematical discourse and practice.

title: The effect of a script and a structured interface in grounding discussions
summary_haiku: This study examined how collaboration scripts and structured interfaces support grounding discussions among international students working remotely. Using a three-condition experiment (unscripted, script-only, script+interface), 42 students performed two grounding discussions structured into input, discussion, and consensus phases. Results showed scripts increased knowledge input quantity and discussion of differences, while structured interfaces further enhanced input length and adherence to prescribed activity sequences. However, no significant effects emerged for summary quality or learning outcomes.

title: Supporting students’ participation in authentic proof activities in computer supported collaborative learning (CSCL) environments Diler Öner
summary_haiku: This paper proposes integrating dynamic geometry software with knowledge-building pedagogy in CSCL environments to support high school students' mathematical proof activities. The author argues that proof instruction should incorporate both empirical exploration and deductive reasoning, reflecting authentic mathematical practice. The study recommends software modifications, particularly adding shared dynamic geometry components and problematizing mechanisms, to help students distinguish between empirical conviction and formal proof while engaging in collaborative knowledge construction.

title: Book review: Exploring thinking as communicating in CSCL
summary_haiku: Sfard's theory conceptualizes mathematical objects as products of discursive processes rather than mental acquisitions, arguing that deep understanding emerges through participation in social routines of mathematical discourse. The review examines how students collaboratively construct mathematical meaning through communication, proposing that extending this participationist framework to computer-mediated group interaction could advance CSCL research while requiring integration with broader social and cultural dimensions.

title: CSCL practices
summary_haiku: This editorial examines computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) practices across educational contexts. It synthesizes research on how collaborative learning emerges through technology-mediated interactions at individual, group, and community levels. Key findings address student self-efficacy in science, game-based math learning outcomes, and automated analysis methods for collaborative discourse, emphasizing that effective CSCL implementation requires attention to surrounding pedagogical and social practices.

title: Leveraging online communities in fostering adaptive schools
authors: David Hung & Kenneth Y. T. Lim & Der-Thanq Victor Chen & Thiam Seng Koh
summary_haiku: Online communities function as "para-communities" that should remain distinct from formal schools rather than being integrated into them. Through conceptual analysis, the authors argue that schools and online communities serve fundamentally different goals: schools emphasize intentional learning and efficiency, while online communities prioritize intrinsic motivation and innovation. They propose that adaptive schools leverage external para-communities through internal Communities of Interest, enabling complementary relationships that cultivate social capital and innovation without compromising organizational efficiency.

title: The right tool for the wrong task? Match and mismatch between first and second stimulus in double stimulation
summary_haiku: This study examines how Norwegian high school students learning English as a foreign language approach open-ended collaborative tasks using wiki technology. Using Vygotsky's double stimulation framework, researchers analyzed the relationship between task design (first stimulus) and available tools (second stimulus) in collaborative knowledge construction. Findings reveal that learners struggled to maintain awareness across individual, group, and whole-class levels. When the wiki application failed, students sustained collective working practices through alternative tools like PowerPoint and MSN chat, demonstrating that pedagogical and technological designs must be better aligned to support collaborative knowledge production.

title: Exploring embedded guidance and self-efficacy in educational multi-user virtual environments
authors: Brian C. Nelson & Diane Jass Ketelhut
summary_haiku: This exploratory study examined how student self-efficacy in scientific inquiry affects guidance system use and learning outcomes in River City, an educational multi-user virtual environment. Using a sample of 96 middle school students, researchers found that students with low self-efficacy viewed significantly fewer guidance messages than higher-efficacy peers. While embedded reflective guidance improved learning across all efficacy levels, it only partially mitigated low self-efficacy's negative impact on performance. Notably, low-efficacy students with heavy guidance use achieved comparable outcomes to high-efficacy students without guidance.

title: Alternative goal structures for computer game-based learning
summary_haiku: This field study examined how cooperative, competitive, and individualistic goal structures in classroom computer math games affect fifth-graders' math performance and attitudes. Using a pretest-posttest design with 160 students across four conditions, results showed all gaming groups outperformed controls on math tests, but cooperative goal structures proved most effective for promoting positive math attitudes. Socioeconomic status significantly moderated outcomes, with disadvantaged students benefiting most from cooperation.

title: Automatic coding of dialogue acts in collaboration protocols
summary_haiku: Researchers developed an automatic coding system to identify dialogue acts (communicative functions) in online collaboration protocols using discourse markers. Testing on 1,000 messages showed 79% agreement with manual coding (Cohen's kappa=0.75). Validity analyses confirmed the system reliably distinguished gender differences in communication patterns and detected experimental intervention effects, supporting its utility for analyzing collaborative learning processes.

title: Yes we can!
summary_haiku: Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) offers transformative potential for education by moving beyond traditional knowledge transfer to engage students in collaborative knowledge construction with peers. This editorial argues that CSCL systems, when fully developed, can provide effective learning environments supporting cross-border collaboration while preparing students for an increasingly global, interdependent world.

title: The pedagogical challenges to collaborative technologies
summary_haiku: # Summary Collaborative technologies rarely address formal learning needs despite their educational potential. This paper proposes the Conversational Framework—a pedagogical model integrating instructionism, constructionism, socio-cultural, and collaborative learning theories—to establish user requirements for technology design. The framework emphasizes iterative interactions between teachers, learners, and peers across discursive and experiential levels, enabling educators to challenge technologies to deliver genuinely enhanced learning rather than merely digitizing conventional methods.

title: Productive failure in CSCL groups
summary_ollama: This study investigated the productive failure hypothesis, which suggests that students who experience failure while working on ill-structured problems in a collaborative learning environment may outperform their peers who worked on well-structured problems. The researchers randomly assigned 177 11th-grade science students to either an ill-structured problem-solving condition or a well-structured problem-solving condition and found that the students in the ill-structured condition performed significantly better on both the well-structured and ill-structured posttests, demonstrating confirmatory evidence for the productive failure hypothesis.
summary_haiku: Groups solving unstructured physics problems without support struggled initially but subsequently outperformed peers who solved well-structured problems on individual transfer tasks. This confirmatory study with 177 eleventh-grade students demonstrates productive failure: complex, divergent collaborative processes seemingly leading to failure paradoxically enhanced later problem-solving performance, suggesting that the nature of collaborative interaction rather than prior knowledge or solution quality drives learning gains.

title: A connective ethnography of peer knowledge sharing and diffusion in a tween virtual world
authors: Deborah A. Fields & Yasmin B. Kafai
summary_haiku: Researchers used connective ethnography to trace how tweens ages 9-12 learned and shared an insider gaming practice—teleporting—across an after-school club, classrooms, and the virtual world Whyville.net. Integrating video, field notes, logfiles, and interviews, they found that most participants traversed multiple physical and virtual spaces to learn this practice, employing observation, questioning, and peer coaching. Knowledge diffusion occurred through informal, unstructured interactions rather than explicit instruction, demonstrating how virtual spaces expand peer-to-peer learning opportunities beyond traditional classroom boundaries.

title: Learning to collaborate while being scripted or by observing a model
authors: Nikol Rummel & Hans Spada & Sabine Hauser
summary_haiku: Observing a worked-out collaboration model with elaboration support proved most effective for improving computer-mediated collaborative problem-solving among medical and psychology students. Using an experimental design with five conditions, researchers found that model-based learning outperformed scripted collaboration on process quality and knowledge measures. Results challenge the prevailing positive view of collaboration scripts in CSCL research, suggesting adaptive scripting approaches instead.

title: The power of natural frameworks: Technology and the question of agency in CSCL settings
summary_haiku: # Summary This study analyzes how secondary school students frame computer-supported collaborative learning situations using video analysis of mathematics problem-solving with educational software. Results reveal students shift between social frameworks where they assume responsibility for understanding tasks and natural frameworks where they attribute difficulties to technology design. When receiving incorrect feedback without explanation, students often cease engaging with mathematical reasoning and instead attempt procedural workarounds, potentially avoiding accountability for learning while preserving self-esteem.

title: Practice perspectives in CSCL
summary_haiku: This editorial argues that CSCL research should adopt practice perspectives to understand how collaborative learning emerges at individual, group, and community levels. Rather than studying interaction through controlled variables and statistical regularities, practice perspectives focus on how people actually interact, examining embodied and materially mediated human activity. The issue's articles demonstrate this approach by analyzing group coordination practices, technology affordances relative to user interaction potential, genre adaptation in virtual environments, and metaskills required for knowledge-creation practices.

title: The joint organization of interaction within a multimodal CSCL medium
authors: Murat Perit Çakır & Alan Zemel & Gerry Stahl
summary_haiku: This ethnomethodological case study examines how three students organize collaborative mathematical problem-solving in a synchronous dual-interaction online environment combining text chat and shared whiteboard. Through sequential interaction analysis, the authors reveal that students co-construct shared mathematical understanding by coordinating visual, narrative, and symbolic representations across media. The indexical field formed by referential links between chat messages and whiteboard drawings establishes common ground, enabling group cognition and deep mathematical learning through multiple realizations of mathematical objects.

title: Affordances revisited: Articulating a Merleau-Pontian view
summary_haiku: This article develops a Merleau-Pontian account of affordances for CSCL, arguing that existing interpretations within the field contain unresolved ontological and epistemological tensions. The author proposes that affordances are dynamic, relational, and skill-relative properties existing independently of perception but relative to agents' body-schematic interaction potential. This framework shifts design and empirical research focus toward background structuring and learners' developing capabilities rather than mental models.

title: Genre and CSCL: The form and rhetoric of the online posting
summary_haiku: This study applies genre analysis to online discussion postings in CSCL contexts, hypothesizing that educational postings share rhetorical characteristics with their epistolary precursor, the letter. Through content analysis of 136 postings, the author identifies 240 rhetorical markers reflecting epistolary dynamics, including salutations, present-tense references, and temporal references. Findings suggest that cultural and historical factors embedded in familiar genres significantly shape how students engage in online collaborative learning, beyond technological affordances alone.

title: Exploring metaskills of knowledge-creating inquiry in higher education
summary_haiku: This study investigates metaskills required for knowledge-creating inquiry in higher education through an 11-week undergraduate psychology course using progressive inquiry and web-based collaboration. Qualitative analysis of database discourse and student self-reflections revealed three student groups exhibited varying engagement levels in collaborative object-oriented inquiry. Group C demonstrated superior skills in monitoring individual, collective, and object-oriented aspects of inquiry, while Groups A and B struggled with shared knowledge advancement. Findings suggest metaskills for collaborative knowledge creation develop through sustained socialization into inquiry practices emphasizing iterative development of shared epistemic objects.

title: A knowledge-practice perspective on technology-mediated learning
summary_haiku: Technology enhances learning through transformed social practices, not merely through tool implementation. While knowledge-building theory emphasizes idea advancement, this perspective argues that genuine educational transformation requires cultivating epistemic practices—socially embedded ways of working with knowledge—that channel intellectual efforts toward collective knowledge advancement. Material artifacts and social practices constitute dialectical unity in knowledge creation.

title: Classical dialogs in CSCL
summary_haiku: This editorial reviews the International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning's progress and synthesizes key research themes from the 2009 CSCL conference. It examines diverse analytical methodologies for studying collaborative learning processes, including event-centered approaches, knowledge creation discourse analysis, and interaction analysis in dual-interaction environments. The authors highlight fundamental tensions between individual and community-level learning, emphasizing how CSCL research must integrate multiple theoretical perspectives and analytical approaches to understand complex collaborative learning phenomena.

title: Time is precious: Variable- and event-centred approaches to process analysis in CSCL research
summary_haiku: CSCL research often neglects temporal dimensions despite studying processes unfolding over weeks or months. Reimann argues that variable-centered variance theory inadequately captures long-term change, proposing event-centered analysis as a complementary approach. Event-based methods enable narrative explanation, accommodate multiple causality types, and facilitate integration of qualitative and quantitative analyses, offering CSCL researchers more appropriate tools for analyzing extended collaborative learning processes.

title: Distinguishing knowledge-sharing, knowledge- construction, and knowledge-creation discourses Jan van Aalst
authors: construction, and knowledge-creation discourses Jan van Aalst
summary_haiku: This study distinguishes three discourse modes—knowledge sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge creation—using a coding scheme applied to secondary students' asynchronous online discussions in Knowledge Forum about SARS and Avian Flu. Analysis of four student groups' discourses revealed one group engaged in knowledge-creation discourse with superior knowledge advancement, one in knowledge-sharing discourse, and two in hybrid modes. Community sense emerged as the primary differentiating factor.

title: A three-level analysis of collaborative learning in dual-interaction spaces
summary_haiku: This article presents a three-level qualitative interaction analysis methodology for dual-interaction spaces—CSCL systems combining shared artifact editing with synchronous communication. The approach analyzes collaborative learning traces at dialog, knowledge, and action levels to identify patterns and inform system customization. Applied to software engineering diagram construction, the method reveals how learners negotiate categorization rules through prototypical examples, enabling evidence-based improvements to learning environment design.

title: Collaborative corrections with spelling control: Digital resources and peer assistance
summary_haiku: Swedish eighth-graders collaboratively corrected spelling errors using Microsoft Word's spellchecker during English writing tasks. Through conversation analysis of video-recorded sessions, the study identified how diagnostic tools and spelling lists configured different correction practices. Students preferentially used diagnostic feedback for autonomous problem-solving before requesting peer assistance or spelling suggestions, demonstrating that underspecified software instructions created space for creative collaborative engagement and language learning.

title: Web 2.0: Inherent tensions and evident challenges for education
summary_haiku: Web 2.0 practices and educational systems embody fundamentally incompatible learning metaphors. While Web 2.0 emphasizes participatory, distributed knowledge construction with internal goals, education prioritizes individual knowledge acquisition for external purposes. This conceptual tension manifests practically in challenges regarding collaboration, evaluation criteria, and material authenticity when Web 2.0 tools are integrated into educational settings.

title: Paradigms of shared knowledge
summary_haiku: This article identifies four theoretical paradigms for understanding shared knowledge in computer-supported collaborative learning: sharing individual mental representations, sharing an object, sharing a situation, and sharing a community. The authors argue that researchers' implicit or explicit adoption of these paradigms significantly influences educational intervention design and effectiveness, regardless of whether designers consciously recognize their theoretical assumptions about knowledge sharing.

title: Wikis to support the “collaborative” part of collaborative learning
summary_haiku: Wikis provide an effective platform for supporting asynchronous, non-collocated collaborative learning when enhanced with awareness, navigation, and communication components. Two case studies demonstrate that prefabricated wiki structures function as coordinating representations, enabling both tightly coupled team design projects and loosely coupled co-blogging activities to maintain adequate intersubjective spaces for productive student collaboration.

title: Earth science learning in SMALLab: A design experiment for mixed reality
summary_haiku: This design experiment examined how mixed-reality environments support collaborative earth science learning. Researchers implemented SMALLab, a semi-immersive platform enabling colocated students to interact face-to-face within computationally mediated spaces. A 3-day intervention with 72 high school students revealed significantly increased student-to-student exchanges compared to traditional instruction and notable achievement gains on concept assessments, suggesting mixed-reality technology's potential for enhancing K-12 collaborative learning when properly designed.

title: Contrasting the use of tools for presentation and critique: Some cases from architectural education
authors: Gustav Lymer & Jonas Ivarsson & Oskar Lindwall
summary_haiku: This ethnomethodological video analysis of architectural design reviews examines how presentation technologies shape critique practices. Comparing poster-based, digital slideshow, and hybrid setups across 143 sessions, the study reveals that digital technologies fundamentally transform sequential organization, shared attention, and part-whole relations during discussion and assessment. The findings suggest that presentation tools designed primarily for delivery may inadequately support subsequent critique, highlighting the need for spatially organized interfaces better suited to collaborative design review practices.

title: An ontology engineering approach to the realization of theory-driven group formation
authors: Seiji Isotani & Akiko Inaba & Mitsuru Ikeda & Riichiro Mizoguchi
summary_haiku: This research presents an ontology-based framework for theory-driven group formation in collaborative learning. Using ontological engineering, the authors formalize learning theory concepts to guide group composition, role assignment, and activity design. A proof-of-concept experiment with four instructors and twenty participants demonstrated that groups formed according to pedagogical theory specifications showed significantly better performance and more meaningful interactions than control groups, suggesting ontologies effectively operationalize learning theories for improved collaborative learning outcomes.

title: The CSCL field matures
summary_haiku: Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) has matured as a field, evidenced by the International Journal of CSCL's acceptance into Thomson Reuters' Web of Science indexing. This editorial reflects on the field's institutional growth since 1989, highlighting how current research demonstrates increased theoretical sophistication, methodological rigor, and productive engagement across diverse disciplinary perspectives within CSCL scholarship.

title: A framework for conceptualizing, representing, and analyzing distributed interaction
authors: Daniel D. Suthers & Nathan Dwyer & Richard Medina & Ravi Vatrapu
summary_haiku: # Summary Suthers and colleagues present an uptake analysis framework for analyzing distributed technology-mediated interaction. The framework uses contingency graphs—abstract transcripts representing events as vertices and relationships between events as edges—to unify interaction data across multiple media and temporal scales. Uptake, defined as participants taking prior events as relevant for ongoing activity, serves as the conceptual foundation. The authors demonstrate the framework's utility through qualitative and quantitative analyses of synchronous and asynchronous collaborative learning data, arguing it enables both microanalysis and scaled statistical analysis while supporting dialogue across diverse CSCL methodologies.

title: Computer-supported argumentation: A review of the state of the art
authors: Oliver Scheuer & Frank Loll & Niels Pinkwart & Bruce M. McLaren
summary_haiku: Computer-supported argumentation systems have evolved over 15-20 years to support and teach argumentation skills across domains. This literature review examines 50 systems, analyzing argument representations, interaction designs, ontologies, automated analysis techniques, and empirical findings. Key results show that visual representations and structured interaction designs improve argumentative discourse, while macro-level pedagogical scripts enhance learning outcomes. However, conflicting empirical results reveal the need for comprehensive theoretical frameworks and systematic comparative studies.

title: Exploring whether students’ use of labelling depends upon the type of activity
authors: Eva Mary Bures & Philip C. Abrami & Richard F. Schmid
summary_haiku: This mixed-methods study examined whether graduate students use labeling features less frequently during structured versus unstructured online dialogue. Participants (n=37) engaged in two activities: an unstructured discussion and a HipBone Game with predetermined structure. Results showed significantly reduced label usage during the structured activity, with 62% using labels multiple times unstructured versus 46% structured. Students preferred the structured dialogue but reported mixed satisfaction with labeling. Findings suggest structured activities provide alternative scaffolding, potentially rendering labeling features redundant.

title: Toward a dialectic relation between the results in CSCL: Three critical methodological aspects of content analysis schemes
summary_haiku: This paper proposes a framework of indicators based on three critical methodological aspects—units of analysis, relations between theoretical levels, and dimensions of analysis—to facilitate reciprocal positioning of content analysis results in CSCL research. Rather than seeking theoretical integration across diverse approaches, the authors argue for dialectical relations that reveal tensions and enable mutual theoretical development within the field's inherent methodological diversity.

title: A prism of CSCL research
summary_haiku: Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning integrates diverse disciplines, technologies, and methodologies to study collaborative learning with digital tools. This issue presents five empirical studies examining different CSCL applications—from complex system simulations to scripted collaboration platforms—using varied analytical approaches including classroom assessments, discourse analysis, and quantitative-qualitative combinations. The research demonstrates that effective CSCL design requires attention to pedagogical aims and collaborative processes rather than relying on single technological solutions.

title: Mr. Vetro: A Collective Simulation for teaching health science
authors: Andri Ioannidou & Alexander Repenning & David Webb & Diane Keyser & Lisa Luhn & Christof Daetwyler
summary_haiku: Mr. Vetro is a collective simulation where students collaboratively control physiological organs on networked computers to learn about system interactions. Formal evaluation across 400 high school students demonstrated significant learning gains in physiological knowledge and vocabulary, increased inquiry-based teaching practices, and positive real-life health behavior changes, though attitudes toward science remained relatively stable.

title: Animation and grammar in science education: Learners’ construal of animated educational software Göran Karlsson
summary_haiku: This case study examines how two upper-secondary students collaboratively interpret animated biochemical processes through written reports. Using interaction analysis of video-recorded sessions, the research reveals that students' grammatically constructed narratives prioritize perceptually salient animated features as active subjects, deriving noun phrases from animation and educational text while substituting verbs with everyday language. Without sufficient subject-matter knowledge, students cannot evaluate adequacy and rely solely on grammatical correctness, resulting in non-scientific explanations. The findings emphasize that technology-supported science education requires consideration of both cultural and semiotic processes.

title: Scripting a distance-learning university course: Do students benefit from net-based scripted collaboration?
summary_haiku: This experimental field study examined whether scripted collaboration benefits net-based learning in a semester-long university operating systems course. Forty-two student groups performed brainstorming, clustering, and essay-writing tasks either with system-enforced scripts or non-scripted instructions. Results showed no general advantage of scripting for knowledge acquisition or task performance. However, principal component analysis revealed scripting slightly improved essay coherence and comprehensibility, suggesting benefits for complex tasks requiring deeper understanding.

title: Distributed leadership in online groups
summary_haiku: In an asynchronous online learning environment, pre-service teachers working in small groups demonstrated highly distributed leadership across all members, with different leadership forms showing varying distribution patterns. While successful group performance was not directly predicted by overall leadership distribution patterns, qualitative analysis revealed that effective groups developed internal organizational structures and positive interpersonal dynamics that facilitated both peer and instructor engagement, suggesting emergent distributed leadership offers a viable alternative to scripted collaborative roles.

title: Promoting metacognitive skills through peer scaffolding in a CSCL environment
summary_haiku: A longitudinal case study of 18 university students using the KnowCat knowledge-building system over two semesters examined how peer scaffolding develops metacognitive skills in computer-supported collaborative learning. Content analysis of student annotations revealed statistically significant increases in metacognitive processes, particularly in monitoring and clarity-seeking behaviors. Results suggest pedagogical use of CSCL environments with structured peer feedback effectively enhances students' self-regulation and collaborative problem-solving capabilities.

title: Guiding group cognition in CSCL
summary_haiku: # Summary CSCL research aims to understand how multiple individuals coalesce into coherent group cognition through collaborative learning. This article examines theoretical frameworks and empirical studies investigating influences on group interaction, including scaffolding strategies, technology support, knowledge sharing mechanisms, and interpersonal trust. The research demonstrates that effective collaboration requires careful attention to sequential interaction, contextual factors, and internal preconditions for productive teamwork.

title: Online moderation of synchronous e-argumentation
authors: Christa S. C. Asterhan & Baruch B. Schwarz
summary_haiku: This exploratory study examines effective online moderation of synchronous small-group argumentation in co-located classrooms. Through student questionnaires and protocol analyses of moderated discussions using Digalo software, researchers found that generic scaffolding prompts—effective in face-to-face settings—were ineffective in synchronous e-discussions. Instead, content-specific, involved moderation styles that disguised scaffolding as peer participation proved more effective and appreciated by students.

title: Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools
authors: Jingyan Lu & Susanne P. Lajoie & Jeffrey Wiseman
summary_haiku: Interactive whiteboards fundamentally altered teacher scaffolding in medical problem-based learning. This case study compared traditional whiteboard versus interactive whiteboard conditions during deteriorating patient simulations with medical students. Results revealed that interactive whiteboards enabled teachers to visualize all student groups' work simultaneously, allowing them to increase problem complexity and reduce task-structuring guidance. Technology expanded scaffolding choices by externalizing collaborative problem-solving processes.

title: How digital concept maps about the collaborators’ knowledge and information influence computer-supported collaborative problem solving
summary_haiku: Digital concept maps displaying collaborators' knowledge structures and information resources enhance computer-supported collaborative problem-solving. This experimental study compared 40 triads—20 with access to partners' concept maps and 20 without—on problem-solving tasks. Results demonstrated that groups with map access acquired greater knowledge-and-information awareness, focused on problem-relevant information, and solved problems faster and more accurately than control groups.

title: S-COL: A Copernican turn for the development of flexibly reusable collaboration scripts
authors: Christof Wecker & Karsten Stegmann & Florian Bernstein & Michael J. Huber & Georg Kalus & Ingo Kollar & Sabine Rathmayer & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: S-COL is a browser-based tool enabling flexible reuse of collaboration scripts across diverse web-based learning platforms. Rather than embedding scripts within specific platforms, S-COL implements scripts in the browser and triggers them by recognizing functionally equivalent page types. An empirical study demonstrated that a collaboration script for online search implemented in S-COL effectively increased students' engagement in early-stage search activities, supporting the tool's feasibility for sustainable script development and reuse.

title: Revealing preconditions for trustful collaboration in CSCL
summary_haiku: This philosophical analysis examines preconditions for trust in virtual learning environments. Through phenomenological inquiry and case analysis, the author argues that self-surrender—fundamental to human communication—is undermined by surveillance and impression management in online learning systems. Drawing on open-source community models, the study concludes that volunteerism, self-articulation of goals, and inquiry-based teaching methods can foster mastery-oriented learning and authentic collaborative engagement.

title: Beyond folk theories of CSCL
summary_haiku: Stahl and Hesse critique three approaches to CSCL research, arguing that the most productive approach develops theories specifically tailored to collaborative learning's unique characteristics. They contend that CSCL requires elaborated theories addressing multiple interpenetrating levels—individual, group, classroom—and technological mediation, moving beyond folk theories and borrowed frameworks to capture phenomena distinctive to computer-supported contexts.

title: Can the interactive whiteboard support young children’s collaborative communication and thinking in classroom science activities?
authors: Ruth Kershner & Neil Mercer & Paul Warwick & Judith Kleine Staarman
summary_haiku: Interactive whiteboards can support young children's collaborative communication and thinking in primary science, but effectiveness depends on multiple interacting factors. Through observational analysis of twelve classrooms, researchers found the IWB facilitates productive dialogue when combined with teacher scaffolding, established "talk rules," and appropriate classroom participation structures. However, the technology alone is not pedagogically transformative; success requires careful integration with other classroom resources and attention to both social and cognitive dimensions of collaborative learning.

title: Sharing and cultivating tacit knowledge in an online learning environment
summary_haiku: Online graduate business students cultivated tacit knowledge through a strategic management course using naturalistic inquiry methodology. The course combined readings, threaded discussions, and a simulation game, creating a "ba" (shared context) that encouraged socialization, externalization, combination, and internalization processes aligned with Nonaka's knowledge creation model. Students reported learning tacit dimensions impossible to acquire from textbooks alone.

title: Using activity theory to understand intergenerational play: The case of Family Quest
authors: Sinem Siyahhan & Sasha A. Barab & Michael P. Downton
summary_haiku: # Summary This study examined intergenerational play between parents and children (ages 9-13) using Quest Atlantis, an educational 3D game, through activity theory analysis.
